title: Business Case Analysis
description: Passage-based case studies to practice reading and decision-making

passages.title: Aurora Analytics — Pricing Pivot
passages.passage:
Aurora Analytics, a five-year-old SaaS company, serves mid-market e-commerce businesses with a real-time customer insights platform. For the past three years, the company has charged a flat $399/month per customer, regardless of usage. Revenue growth has been steady at 18% year-over-year, but two trends are concerning leadership:

First, large customers — those processing millions of events monthly — are heavily discounted in negotiation, with the average enterprise deal closing at $240/month. These customers consume the most infrastructure and account for 68% of compute costs while contributing only 41% of revenue.

Second, smaller customers (under 50,000 events/month) churn at 4.2% monthly, citing the price as 'too high for what we use.' The CFO has proposed three alternatives: (a) a tiered plan with $99 / $399 / $899 buckets based on event volume, (b) pure usage-based pricing at $0.002 per event with a $49 minimum, or (c) a hybrid: $99 base plus $0.001 per event over 100,000.

The head of engineering warns that pure usage-based pricing would make revenue 'lumpy and hard to forecast,' while the head of sales worries that tiered plans will trigger price-anchoring negotiations on the top tier.

questions.question: Based on the passage, what is the primary financial risk of the current flat-rate model?
options: Small customers are subsidizing the cost of large customers
Large customers are unprofitable relative to the infrastructure they consume
Pricing is too low to support the engineering team
Customers cannot predict their monthly bill
questions.explanation: The passage states large customers contribute 41% of revenue but consume 68% of compute costs — a clear sign that they are a margin drag. Small customers churning is a separate, retention concern.

questions.question: Which of the proposed options best addresses BOTH the enterprise margin issue and small-customer churn simultaneously?
options: Tiered $99 / $399 / $899 buckets
Pure usage at $0.002/event with $49 minimum
Hybrid: $99 base + $0.001/event over 100,000
Keep flat pricing but raise it to $599
questions.explanation: The hybrid model lowers the entry price (helps small-customer churn) and scales cost with usage (recoups margin from heavy users), without making revenue purely volatile. Pure usage-based would solve margin but worsen forecast volatility per the engineering head's concern.

questions.question: The head of sales worries tiered plans will trigger 'price-anchoring' on the top tier. What does this concern mean?
options: Customers will refuse to pay any price above the lowest tier
Customers will use the top-tier price as a starting point to negotiate discounts down
Sales reps will be forced to upsell aggressively
The top tier will become the default expected price
questions.explanation: Price anchoring in sales negotiation refers to customers latching onto a visible high price and pushing down from it — exactly what the head of sales is warning about. Option D describes a different psychology effect.

questions.question: Which metric most directly measures product stickiness?
options: MRR
NPS
DAU/MAU ratio
Churn rate
questions.explanation: DAU/MAU (daily over monthly active users) directly captures how frequently users return — the textbook 'stickiness' metric.

passages.title: Helix Health — Onboarding Crisis
passages.passage:
Helix Health, a telemedicine platform, recently discovered that 62% of new patient signups never complete their first consultation. Investigation revealed that the onboarding flow requires patients to: (1) verify their email, (2) upload a government ID, (3) connect their insurance, (4) fill a 32-field medical history form, and (5) schedule their first appointment.

Analytics show 41% of dropouts occur at step 4 (the medical history form). A junior PM proposes shortening the form to 8 fields. The head of clinical operations objects: 'We legally need that information before a doctor can consult.' The CTO counters: 'We can collect it later, just not at signup.'

questions.question: What is the strongest argument for the CTO's proposal to defer the medical history form?
options: It would reduce engineering load
Information collected later — even right before the consult — still satisfies the legal requirement
Patients don't actually need medical history for a telemedicine visit
The junior PM has more product experience
questions.explanation: The clinical objection is about WHEN the info is collected, not whether. The CTO's point is that as long as it's gathered before the consult, the legal/clinical requirement is met — and moving it out of signup removes a 41% drop-off point.

questions.question: If Helix could only run one experiment first, which would yield the most signal about onboarding friction?
options: A/B test the email verification copy
Move the medical history form to immediately before the first consult
Add a progress bar to all five steps
Remove the government ID requirement entirely
questions.explanation: The 41% drop at step 4 is the largest single source of dropout. Moving it directly tests the deferral hypothesis. Other changes target much smaller potential gains.
